'''Diagnostic substitution''' is a phenomenon in which one label for a condition becomes replaced with another, causing an apparent decrease in the rate of the first condition and increase in the rate of the second.<ref>{{cite book |pages = 944–945| author=Shattuck, Paul| title=Encyclopedia of Autism Spectrum Disorders| chapter=Diagnostic Substitution| doi=10.1007/978-1-4419-1698-3_5 |year = 2013|isbn = 978-1-4419-1697-6}}</ref> 

==Autism==
The best-known example is that of the increasing rates of [[autism]] in developed countries such as the United States, which some studies suggest is at least partly a result of people substituting diagnoses of autism for [[intellectual disability]] and [[learning disabilities]].<ref name=Shattuck>{{Cite journal | last1 = Shattuck | first1 = P. T. | title = The Contribution of Diagnostic Substitution to the Growing Administrative Prevalence of Autism in US Special Education | doi = 10.1542/peds.2005-1516 | journal = Pediatrics | volume = 117 | issue = 4 | pages = 1028–1037 | year = 2006 | pmid =  16585296| s2cid = 26733990 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal 
| last1 = Coo | first1 = H. 
| last2 = Ouellette-Kuntz | first2 = H. L. N. 
| last3 = Lloyd | first3 = J. E. V. 
| last4 = Kasmara | first4 = L. 
| last5 = Holden | first5 = J. J. A. 
| last6 = Lewis | first6 = M. E. S. 
| doi = 10.1007/s10803-007-0478-x

| volume = 38

Institute]] |title=Report to the legislature on the principal findings of the epidemiology of autism in California: a comprehensive pilot study |year=2002 |url=http://www.ucdmc.ucdavis.edu/mindinstitute/newsroom/study_final.pdf |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080414094255/http://www.ucdmc.ucdavis.edu/mindinstitute/newsroom/study_final.pdf |archive-date=2008-04-14 |name-list-style=vanc |author2=Sage AC |author3=Keyzer J |display-authors=3  |author4=<Please add first missing authors to populate metadata.> }}</ref> this study used data from the [[California Department of Developmental Services]] database, which, according to a study by [[Paul Shattuck]], is unreliable because "...the administrative prevalence figures for most states are well below epidemiological estimates."<ref name=Shattuck/> With regard to the role of diagnostic substitution in the increase in reported cases of autism, [[Dorothy Bishop (psychologist)|Dorothy Bishop]] has said, "This could be in part because of new conceptualisations of autism, but may also be fuelled by strategic considerations: resources for children with ASD tend to be much better than those for children with other related conditions, such as language impairment or intellectual handicaps, so this diagnosis may be preferred."<ref>{{cite web | url=https://deevybee.blogspot.co.uk/2012/06/autism-epidemic-and-diagnostic.html | title=The 'autism epidemic' and diagnostic substitution | work=Deevybee.blogspot.co.uk | date=4 June 2012 | access-date=9 October 2013 | author=Bishop, Dorothy}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2012/06/you-say-semantic-pragmatic-disorder-i-say-autism/258077/ | title=You say 'Semantic-Pragmatic Disorder,' I Say 'Autism' | work=[[The Atlantic]] | date=4 June 2012 | access-date=9 October 2013 | author=Fung, Brian}}</ref> Bishop has herself published a small study concluding that people who would now be diagnosed as autistic would, in the past, have been diagnosed with [[developmental language disorder]].<ref>{{Cite journal | last1 = Bishop | first1 = D. V. M. | last2 = Whitehouse | first2 = A. J. O. | last3 = Watt | first3 = H. J. | last4 = Line | first4 = E. A. | title = Autism and diagnostic substitution: Evidence from a study of adults with a history of developmental language disorder | doi = 10.1111/j.1469-8749.2008.02057.x | journal = Developmental Medicine & Child Neurology | volume = 50 | issue = 5 | pages = 341–45 | year = 2008 | pmid =  18384386| doi-access = free }}</ref> [[Emily Willingham]] has noted that at the time autism was first reported by [[Leo Kanner]] in 1943, while autistic people existed before that time, they had historically been referred to as insane, [[schizophrenic]], intellectually disabled, or language impaired.<ref>{{cite web | url=http://www.boston.com/bostonglobe/ideas/brainiac/2012/07/autism_not_actu.html | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120727235312/http://www.boston.com/bostonglobe/ideas/brainiac/2012/07/autism_not_actu.html | url-status=dead | archive-date=July 27, 2012 | title=Autism: Not Actually on the Rise | work=[[Boston.com]] | date=25 July 2012 | access-date=9 October 2013 | author=Rothman, Josh}}</ref>
